title: Heavy Attrition
fit_question: Describe your leadership style and an example of when you demonstrated it. Why are you specifically interested in our firm and chosen office?
prompt: A ten-year-old medical-device company has heavy attrition among junior salespeople. New hires stay less than one year even though it takes roughly six months to become effective, while salespeople with more than three years at the company have almost no attrition. Diagnose the causes and recommend a response.

clarifying_info.answer: New hires average less than one year; experienced salespeople with more than three years have almost no attrition.
A salesperson needs about six months to learn the job and become productive.
The medical-device company has operated for ten years.

interviewer_notes: Open-ended partner-style candidate-led case focused on hypothesis formation and structured brainstorming. The intended hypothesis is that junior and senior incentive economics differ. Tasks are similar, so direct the discussion toward commission determinants: products, territory/client potential and travel burden.

suggested_framework.summary: Rule out performance-driven exits and broad work-condition issues, then compare junior and senior incentives and opportunity access.

children.label: Hours, tasks, location, benefits and management
Training, ramp support and career path
Products and commission by margin and effort

stages.interviewer_asks: Where should we start in diagnosing heavy junior-sales attrition?
stages.expected_answer: Define the attrition by cohort, tenure, voluntary status and performance; compare market benchmarks; assess work conditions, manager and career experience; and compare total compensation, commission opportunity, territory quality and travel between junior and senior staff.
good_answer_signals: Uses the junior-versus-senior contrast to prioritize incentives

stages.interviewer_asks: Assuming junior and senior tasks are similar, what determines the incentives they obtain?
stages.expected_answer: Commission depends on which products they may sell and each product's price, margin and effort; the clients and economic potential of assigned territories, including whether accounts are new or established; and the travel time and expense needed to reach customers.
good_answer_signals: Creates at least three clear buckets
Connects each bucket to actual commission opportunity

stages.interviewer_asks: How could product access create attrition?
stages.expected_answer: If juniors can sell only low-price or low-commission devices while seniors control high-margin products, their earnings stay low regardless of effort. Commission rates should reflect margin and selling difficulty, and juniors need a credible path to higher-value products.

stages.interviewer_asks: How could territory and travel assignments create attrition?
stages.expected_answer: Juniors may inherit low-income, low-awareness or new-account territories while seniors retain high-volume relationships. Scattered customers also reduce selling time and raise travel burden. Normalize quotas or commission for territory potential and distance, reimburse expense and rotate or rebalance accounts.
good_answer_signals: Connects distance to selling capacity and pay

stages.expected_answer: Survey recent leavers and current juniors to confirm the cause, then audit product access, territory potential and travel burden by tenure. Redesign commissions and assignments to equalize earning opportunity for comparable effort, involve senior sellers in the redesign and benchmark competitors. Pilot changes while monitoring both junior retention and senior attrition.
good_answer_signals: Balances junior fairness with senior-retention risk

synthesis: The strongest hypothesis is unequal earning opportunity, not different work. Confirm it through exit surveys and a tenure-level audit of product access, territory potential, established accounts, travel and commission. Rebalance assignments and compensate for effort and distance, while involving senior sellers and monitoring whether the redesign shifts attrition upward.
what_great_looks_like: Uses the tenure contrast to focus the diagnosis
Structures product, territory and distance drivers
common_pitfalls: Lists generic morale issues without prioritization
Assumes equal commission rates mean equal opportunity

extraction.notes: The case has no candidate exhibits or calculations; its core is structured qualitative diagnosis and incentive redesign. Reviewed and accepted by Claude 2026-09-30.
